dialogue_history.speaker: grok-3_mas_rag
dialogue_history.sentences_no_utterance_types: Limiting migration ignores our humanitarian duty to support those in need, especially when we can plan better resource allocation to ease public service strain. How do you justify restricting migration as a fix for cost of living pressures when many immigrants contribute through taxes and fill essential roles? Slashing immigration won't fix waiting times or prices; instead, we need government investment in the NHS and welfare to tackle these issues head-on. Instead of stricter enforcement, we should be investing in systems that help manage migration fairly while protecting vulnerable people seeking safety.

dialogue_history.speaker: human_4
dialogue_history.sentences_no_utterance_types: Restricting migration does not mean necessarily stopping migration. What it means is allowing people that will provide a benefit to our society to come, meanwhile turning away those who don't. Skilled workers are more than welcome to the UK as they are more likely to provide a net benefit for the system. However those who cannot provide any value for British society shouldn't be allowed in, as it is likely that the British tax-payer will be funding their stay. This drives up tax and drives up cost of living. Systems like this should be put in place until the cost of living situation and public services situation is stable. This puts people who have lived and worked here first. Once we know this country is able to take care of it's own, we can then assume that it's able to take care of others. Do you not think it's important that the country you are born in is in a position to help you first?

dialogue_history.sentences_no_utterance_types: How can you justify delaying support for vulnerable people fleeing crisis until our own issues are sorted, when we have a moral obligation to help now? Judging people's worth to society based on immediate 'benefit' is a cold-hearted approach that ignores our moral duty to help those in desperate need. Prioritising skilled workers risks creating a system that punishes the vulnerable and forgets that compassion, not just economics, should guide our immigration policies. Delaying support for others until we're 'ready' risks lives and undermines the values of compassion and equity that define us as a nation. A country’s strength in 2025 lies in balancing support for its people with compassion for others, not in shutting the door on those in need.

Compassion will still exist, only it will be independent parties that care more for this.
